newsitem.title: CHINA: WTO chief sees tough talks ahead on China entry.
newsitem.headline: WTO chief sees tough talks ahead on China entry.

text.p: World Trade Organisation chief Renato Ruggiero on Wednesday predicted tough times ahead in talks on China's long-delayed entry to the global trade club, but said he was optimistic Beijing would finally win admission.
"We are approaching now the final stage of the negotiations, and just because of that it will be a tough time," Ruggiero told a news conference.

"Before the end of the spring, the Chinese side has to present an ambitious offer on market access," said the visiting WTO director general, who arrived in Beijing on Sunday after a tour of China's booming economic hub, Shanghai.

Ruggerio said he was trying to inject a sense of urgency and flexibility into talks on China's WTO entry, which has been delayed by differences between Beijing and current members over the terms of its accession.

Diplomats from countries involved in China's crucial bilateral talks on WTO entry say they have seen little change in recent weeks in China's position on fundamental issues holding up its admission, despite progress made in talks in March.

Those issues -- focused on creating a level playing field and ensuring market access -- ranged from opening China's agriculture markets, financial services, insurance and distribution systems to clarifying controversial subsidies to state industry, they said.
"Very difficult issues lie ahead, like agriculture, like services, like transparency, like a transition period," Ruggiero said.
But Ruggiero, who is not involved in the entry negotiations since these take place in bilateral talks and with members en bloc, said there was no basic opposition to China's accession.
"Yes, we have difficulties, but if we concentrate on the process, if from every side we show flexibility and a sense of urgency, it is possible to have a good outcome," he said.
"We are and should remain optimists," he said, adding that no specific date for Beijing's entry had been set.
In meetings with senior Chinese leaders, Ruggiero has cited the progress achieved in bilateral talks in Geneva last March and has urged Beijing to move faster to ensure its admission.

After the March talks, Chinese and Western negotiators said they had made progress on Beijing's 10-year-old application for membership of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade and its successor organisation, the WTO.

The WTO chief said he had received commitments from Chinese leaders that they would continue economic liberalisation, but warned faster progress on WTO entry was essential for Beijing's integration into the world economy.
"They understand perfectly well that in the next months and years, WTO will continue to write the rules that will govern international trade in the 21st century," he said.

Beijing's next opportunity to lay a new offer on the table will come in late May, when non-discrimination -- creating a level playing field -- and ensuring an independent body for judicial review will be among the hottest topics.
"The next negotiation session in May must be at least as positive as the session that we had in March," Ruggiero said.
"Then, in September we can begin the negotiations on the remaining hard-core issues."

Chinese Premier Li Peng on Tuesday told Ruggiero that Beijing's WTO accession should not be politicised, saying that world trade remained unfair and often influenced by power politics, the official People's Daily said.
But Li stressed that China remained committed to gaining WTO entry, the newspaper said.
